title: Important Differences: DPSP vs Fundamental Rights

blocks.content: The Indian Constitution is founded on the bedrock of the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.

rows: Negative; prohibit the State from taking certain actions.
Positive; require the State to perform certain duties.
Non-justiciable; cannot be enforced by any court.
Legal sanctions backed by constitutional remedies.
Moral and political sanctions backed by public opinion.
Promote individual liberty and civil welfare.
Promote community welfare and a socio-economic Welfare State.

items: Champakam Dorairajan Case (1951): The Supreme Court ruled that Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSPs in case of conflict.
25th Constitutional Amendment Act (1971): Inserted Article 31C, giving precedence to DPSPs under Article 39(b) and (c) over Fundamental Rights in Articles 14 and 19.
Minerva Mills Case (1980): The Supreme Court held that the Constitution relies on harmony between Part III and Part IV, and absolute supremacy of one over the other destroys the basic structure.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Fundamental Rights are negative injunctions that prohibit the State from restricting individual liberty, whereas Directive Principles are positive commands requiring the State to take social welfare measures.
Fundamental Rights are legally enforceable and justiciable in court under Articles 32 and 226, while Directive Principles are non-justiciable under Article 37.
Fundamental Rights aim to establish political democracy, whereas Directive Principles aim to establish social and economic democracy.
Fundamental Rights carry legal sanctions, whereas Directive Principles carry moral and political sanctions.
In case of a conflict, courts generally uphold Fundamental Rights, except when laws are enacted to implement Articles 39(b) and 39(c) as protected under Article 31C.
